# Jiffy: Ibotta’s Internal AI Artifact Hosting Platform


## How we helped spark a building culture at Ibotta


[Brett Markowitz](https://medium.com/@brett.markowitz?source=post_page---byline--61d28a403d90---------------------------------------)


4 min read


·


Just now


--


By:[Brett Markowitz](https://medium.com/u/b3c62fbc9828?source=post_page---user_mention--61d28a403d90---------------------------------------)


&[Justin Hart](https://medium.com/u/3bcec7b6ff63?source=post_page---user_mention--61d28a403d90---------------------------------------)


Press enter or click to view image in full size


At Ibotta, we believe good ideas can come from anywhere. We value transparency; we share proactively and build in the open.


LLMs have made it easier than ever to live these values. But one problem remained: once you’ve built something, how do you actually share it with others? Passing around files is clunky and hard to manage. And for one-off ideas or prototypes, it’s usually not worth it to fully provision infrastructure.


Shopify recently shared how they built[Quick](https://shopify.engineering/quick) , an internal platform where anyone can publish a website. There’s also Drop by Vercel, Netlify, GitHub Pages, and other static site platforms.


We were inspired by these projects and love to build, so we set out to create our own, shaped around how Ibotta operates.


In less than a week, a small team built the foundation of Jiffy, Ibotta’s internal platform for hosting AI artifacts. In just two months, over 10% of the company has already created at least one site (also referred to as a Jiffy). There are over 400 Jiffies in total, with more appearing every day.


Here’s how it works and what we’ve learned.


## What makes a Jiffy a Jiffy?


The goal behind Jiffy is to make it easy for anyone at Ibotta to share their ideas. To do this effectively and efficiently, we keep a few principles in mind.


- **Friendly:** Jiffy is for everyone at Ibotta. We’re all builders, regardless of title.
- **Fast:** Anything less is frustrating.
- **Flexible:** Go further (within reason) as needed.
- **Fun:** Keep things light and allow everyone to express themselves.


The design leans into neobrutalist styling alongside the colors of the[Jiffy Pop popcorn brand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiffy_Pop) .


Press enter or click to view image in full size


## A peek behind the foil


Jiffy runs on AWS serverless infrastructure.


All sites live at their own prefix in an S3 bucket behind CloudFront. A Lambda@Edge function ensures only Ibotta employees authenticated through our IdP can view Jiffies.


A Jiffy can be deployed four ways: a CLI, an MCP server for agents, a GitHub Action, and a web frontend (which is itself a Jiffy). The frontend, known as “pop”, lets you browse and upvote other Jiffies, view stats, and read documentation.


The deployment flow is simple. Behind a private API gateway, a Lambda checks if your desired Jiffy name exists, then vends credentials to the client, which uploads files directly to S3. From there, you can redeploy or add editors who can deploy on your behalf.


From there, you can redeploy your Jiffy, or add editors to it who can do so on your behalf.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


For folks who want to go further, we built a handful of integrations backed by Lambda functions:


- Identity, to get the current user’s name, role, and Slack photo
- Persistence, to access a DynamoDB partition for storing data entries
- WebSockets, to enable multiplayer experiences and provide live updates of on-page activity
- Gateways, to safely and securely call third-party APIs, like Jira and GitHub, using credentials stored in Secrets Manager
- File upload, to store user-generated content


Each of these integrations is accessible via an SDK anyone can import into their Jiffy’s code.


The SDK also includes APIs for adding commenting functionality to your Jiffy. Visitors can highlight elements and leave a message, reply to others, and react with emojis.


## Agents at the forefront


The main driver for Jiffy was making it easy to share LLM-generated artifacts. To achieve this, we made sure agents get a first-class experience when interacting with Jiffy. We created a skill that guides agents through Jiffy’s capabilities and an MCP server that manages Jiffies.


The MCP server uses the same authorization mechanisms and shares a common backend codebase with the other systems.


## What’s next


Jiffy has taken on a life of its own. Ibottans use it every day to create and share everything from games to documentation to prototypes. Things that were previously out of reach are now just a few prompts and clicks away.


Next up, we want to make it easier to locate and discover Jiffies, experiment with simple access controls, and expand the capabilities of agents interacting with Jiffy.


If a culture of craft, building, and a bit of jiffery sounds appealing to you, we’re hiring! Check out[our careers page](https://ibotta.com/work-with-us/careers) and consider applying.


Big thank you to the talented engineers at Ibotta who helped bring Jiffy to life — Justin Hart, Joshua Morrisett, Steven Monetti, and Matt Klich.
